lesson.subtitle: Lesson 18 -- The Client Success Story -- Reading a Case Study
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Izabel Cristina de Pieri | Lesson 18 -- The Client Success Story

listenings.text: Good morning, Izabel. It is Sofia, with the numbers the writer asked for, so nothing in the case study is guesswork. Start with the pain point, because that is what the reader remembers: Meridian's warehouse could not trust a sensor that stopped reporting. We took the worst month, February, as the baseline, and we agreed on three metrics with David: uptime, defect rate and time to replacement. Here is what the numbers say. Adoption of the new dashboard climbed from thirty-one percent in January to ninety-four percent in May. Attrition, which had reached two accounts in the quarter of the failure, is now at zero. Implementation was slow on purpose; onboarding forty warehouse operators took us three weeks, and the findings show they trusted the weekly report more than the hardware. The payback period on the firmware rebuild is eleven months. Expensive, yes, but far cheaper than losing the account. Publish all of it, including the numbers that do not flatter us. That is the whole reason the study is credible.

Izabel, it is David Chen at Meridian. Your writer sent me the draft of the case study, and I have read it twice. I will approve it, and I will give you the testimonial, but I want you to know why. It is not because the recovery was fast, because it was not. It is because you published the numbers that made you look bad, right next to the ones that made you look good. The proof of concept arrived before the full shipment, exactly as you said it would. My operators were onboarded properly, not left with a manual. And when I asked for the findings, you sent me the whole file, not a summary. So here is my line, and you may quote it: they told me the date, and then they met it. Send the final version to my legal team by Friday and we will sign off on it. And Izabel, treat this file as a best practice. Do the next account the same way.

reading.rtitle: The Meridian Turnaround: A Case Study
paras: Published six months after the Halo failure, this case study follows the Meridian account from the day the line went down to the day the contract was renewed. The pain point was simple: Meridian's warehouse could not trust a sensor that stopped reporting. Having lost the client's confidence in a single week, AVRT chose not to argue. It measured. Taking the worst month as the baseline, the team agreed on three metrics with David Chen -- uptime, defect rate and time to replacement -- and published them every Thursday.

Rebuilt by an external firm and tested unit by unit, the firmware went back to Meridian as a proof of concept before any full shipment. Implementation was deliberately slow. Onboarding the warehouse staff on the new dashboard, AVRT trained forty operators in three weeks; asked later what had changed, they pointed at the weekly report rather than at the hardware. Adoption climbed from thirty-one percent in January to ninety-four percent in May. Attrition, which had reached two accounts in the quarter of the failure, fell to zero.

The findings are not flattering to AVRT, and that is the point. Read honestly, the case study shows a supplier that recovered because it published its own numbers, including the ugly ones. The payback period on the firmware rebuild was eleven months -- expensive, but far cheaper than losing the account. Asked for a testimonial, David Chen wrote a single line: they told me the date, and then they met it. Having survived the worst quarter in its history, AVRT now treats the Meridian file as a best practice, and every new client is onboarded the same way.
reading.source: Adapted from the AVRT client case study, published with Meridian Distribution

gapfill.text: A participle clause is a shorter way to say why, when or how something happened. -ing (Taking the worst month as the baseline...) replaces an active clause: because we took / while we took. A past participle (Rebuilt by an external firm...) replaces a passive one: because it was rebuilt. Having + past participle (Having lost the account...) marks the EARLIER action. One rule decides everything: the missing subject of the participle must be the subject of the main clause.

lf.text: Three types. -ing = active (Taking the baseline = because we took it). Past participle = passive (Rebuilt by a firm = because it was rebuilt). Having + past participle = the action that came FIRST. In every case the participle belongs to the subject of the main clause, so check that subject before you write the comma.

items: Scenario 1
Open the story with Having + past participle: AVRT lost the confidence first, then chose to measure.
Scenario 2
Explain the baseline with an -ing clause: the team took February as the baseline and agreed on three metrics.
Scenario 3
Describe the firmware with a past participle clause: it was rebuilt by an external firm and sent as a proof of concept.
Scenario 4
Tell the Meridian story to a new client in four sentences, using at least three participle clauses.
